pricing my work is truly my LEAST favourite thing 😭  especially after trying to look closer at the numbers behind my small ceramic business. i’m trying to map out the potential 1, 3, and 5 year revenue and expense projections to see if investing in a kiln and building this business actually makes any sense. at my current $30-$65 price point, i’m losing money selling my work and cannot justify a kiln. i’ve made the terrifying decision to raise my prices by 25-30%. the money will go towards expanding production (investing. in a kiln & shelving), upgrading my website, expanding to ship to the US, and finally, offering private lessons and workshops.  with the price increase, I will still need to survive 6 months - 1 year without a livable wage / making profit. i’ll be focusing on my higher-margin petal bowls and bring in some more affordable $25 products like spoon rests and trinket dishes to keep things as accessible as possible. my mugs are not viable as they take me 2hrs each, but i’m going to keep making them for now and hope i can speed it up. no more lidded jars outside of speciality collections as the margins are too low.  i’m also going to try to secure 1-2 freelance social media clients to provide me with some supplement income as a buffer. this is the behind the scenes of small ceramics business’ that you normally don’t see, because it’s not nearly as cute or fun as the pots themselves. #potterybusiness #ceramics #smallbusiness #priceincrease #handmadeceramics

In my YouTube video this weekend I’m recreating some pots I haven’t thrown since 2014, specially store jars with inset, internal galleries and thin lids with thrown knobs. You can find a link to the fully narrated video via the Linktree in my profile’s biography.   I’ve lied a little bit. I did create jars that were similar to this during my apprenticeship with Lisa Hammond between 2014-2017, yet they were bellied pieces with a gallery closer to the jars I make these days, yet they unusual thrown knobs that were in themselves similar to small bowls.   To create pots with internal galleries like this you need to split the rim. One section becomes the lip, the other is coaxed inside and carefully set horizontal to essentially become a ledge onto which the lid can be held aloft. This alone is a tricky task and it involves throwing a form with enough material in the lip to withstand such a manoeuvre. Secondly, there’s the small disc-like lid, a form that’s thrown off-the-hump and then the following day it’s trimmed back to have its more exacting shape and the knob is thrown on, again, a tricky task as it involves fiddly, fingertip throwing and a lot of accuracy.   All of this and more will be covered in my longer, narrated YouTube upload. I enjoyed making these and since it has been such a long time since I’ve crafted them, my skillset in the interim has improved massively, thus I could apply newly learnt techniques and ability into making shapes I used to struggle with to some degree. I hope you like the film if you happen to click over and watch it, it’s greatly appreciated if you do as it helps to keep the lights on in the workshop.   #pottery #ceramics #handmade #jar #satisfying

videos.caption: I’m a sucker for the making of pots, the joyous throwing and trimming, but what comes after, the waxing, glazing and firing, is more of a laborious task that normally ends up being highly repetitive. I don’t mind the work, I keep my headphones on and listen to stories throughout the day, yet I definitely experience more pain in my hands from these processes, as compared to throwing and trimming. Specifically, it’s the grasping of pots as I fettle the surface clean, as the fingers that are gripped so tightly around the object cannot move, otherwise they rub down the surface and create thin patches that show in the finished pots. This means that the hand that holds the pots is tensed for hours on end with my fingers pressed against a relatively powdery surface, if I squeeze too hard, the clay can fracture and come off of the vessel and too loose a grip means my digits glide across the surface, again creating thin spots. It’s hard to describe, but essentially this hand becomes a vice whilst the other carefully cleans the surface. It’s a skill, just like any other in the making process. #pottery #glazing #glaze #howto #craftsmanship #ceramics

Here’s an easy way to create a bold and dynamic surface design without spending hours nitpicking. This technique starts with a simple cylinder and a handful of slip, but the real magic comes from how the slip is applied while the wheel is spinning. One of the biggest game changers is sieving your slip multiple times before applying it. That silky smooth consistency helps the slip move naturally across the form instead of having clay chunks or inconsistencies. I also like pre-trimming a small foot before adding texture. It catches the excess slip and makes cleanup much easier later by not disturbing the texture during the trimming phase. As the glaze melts over these ridges, it naturally breaks across the high points and exposes flashes of the iron-rich clay underneath. That variation is what gives every single piece its own personality. It’s fast, expressive, and one of my favorite ways to create texture that feels organic and alive. Comment the word “SLIP” if you want my FREE Slip Texturing Starter Guide. 🌀 #pottery #ceramics #slip #texture #potterywheel

If you’d like to see a far more thorough exploration of these vases, I recommend watching the 40-minute version that’s on my YouTube channel, a link to which you can find via the Linktree in my profile’s biography.   This week I’m making some of my favourite pots, they aren’t really about function, at least that is not what I’m thinking about whilst I create them. These angular vases with a protruding line across one side are simple, decorative objects and a welcome change after a few weeks of focusing solely on functional ware. I take my time with them and pay close attention to proportion and surface and how the line travels and over the past few years they’ve changed quite a lot.   They used to appear squatter and the lines were heavier and less defined but after making many batches, they have gradually become taller and more refined, in my opinion. The carved line has followed that shift, it’s sharper now, more deliberate and despite only being a relatively small addition, the change it makes is drastic. Most of my work is thrown on the wheel and naturally symmetrical and therefore this detail interrupts that uniformity. It gives the vessel a direction and a front. It catches the light and throws a shadow across the flat planes and somehow that single line makes the pots feel more figurative, especially when they are grouped together.   If you happen to click over and watch the longer edition, thank you, it means so much!   #pottery #vase #sculpture #handmade #ceramics

One of the questions I get most often is how I keep my ceramic tiles from warping while they dry. My secret is simple: patience and a little sandwiching, hold the mayo. I dry my clay tiles between ware boards for the first couple of days. This helps them dry evenly and stay nice and flat. Once they're past leather hard I move them to drying racks to finish drying. My racks are a mix of cookie cooling racks and shelves salvaged from discarded refrigerators. You don't need anything fancy—use whatever works! The goal is good airflow while supporting your pieces as they dry. It's a simple pottery tip, but it has saved me from a lot of warped tiles over the years. #pottery #ceramics #potterytips #claytips #ceramicart
